title: When Being Nice Means Staying Quiet
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Camilo Zambrano reflects on how a childhood of respecting elders and keeping the peace taught him to equate being nice, kind and agreeable. He traces the habit through school, relationships and work, and names it self-silencing, the act of withholding what he feels out of worry about another's reaction. Drawing on No More Mr. Nice Guy and Radical Candor, he separates the three traits and argues that kindness can coexist with firm boundaries and honest challenge. He adds that boundaries require first knowing what he is protecting and that he must also stay open to feedback, warning against swinging to the opposite extreme. The piece closes with a practical test, asking whether he has actually said what he thinks.
points: Being nice, agreeable and kind are distinct traits that people routinely conflate.
Self-silencing means holding back what you feel to avoid someone's reaction, and it quietly erodes your boundaries.
Radical Candor offers a model in which caring about people and challenging them reinforce each other.
Effective boundaries start with clarity about what you are protecting and are balanced by willingness to hear feedback.
A simple check before agreeing is to ask whether you have actually said what you think.
quotes: For a long time, I thought being nice, being kind, and being agreeable were sort of more or less the same thing.
I had much less practice saying that something bothered me while still treating the other person with respect. Staying quiet was more comfortable, even when it could impact me somehow.

Recently I discovered the term self-silencing, which helped me name that reaction. It’s when you feel or want to say something, but hold it back because you’re worried about the other person’s reaction.

when I think of being nice, I think of being pleasant and considerate in how I interact with someone; being agreeable, on the other hand, brings in a willingness to go along, accommodate, and find common ground; kindness asks me to care about how I treat people and how my actions affect them.
During my time at Amazon, I came across the book Radical Candor, and it really opened my mind to the idea that I can still hold my ground and challenge others while caring about them.
Before I can communicate a limit clearly, I need to know what I’m trying to protect and why it matters.
My values have to guide both the boundaries I set and the changes I’m willing to make.
Now the difference is that before I automatically agree, I want to give myself enough room to ask myself a simple question.
context: Zambrano opens by admitting he long conflated niceness, kindness and agreeableness, which sets up the distinction the essay then draws.
This passage shows how childhood training in compliance left him practiced at keeping the peace but not at voicing discomfort respectfully.
The author names the pattern of withholding one's real view for fear of reaction as self-silencing, giving readers vocabulary for it.
Zambrano defines the three traits separately to show that each has a legitimate role but that conflating them erodes self-awareness.
He cites Radical Candor as the source of the idea that caring about someone and challenging them are compatible rather than opposed.
The author argues that boundaries are first an internal act of clarity about what is being protected, before they are communicated to others.
Zambrano ties boundary setting to personal coherence, insisting values must govern both what he refuses and what he is willing to change.
The closing line turns the essay into a practical habit, a pause to check whether one's own view has actually been voiced.
